messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 23
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside

Vignette:
Asha was 23 when she first came for help, a South Asian woman working as an auditor in the United States, but the story she brought into the room began years earlier, when she was still living in a war zone as a civilian and trying to move through ordinary days while danger had become part of the landscape. She described one afternoon in particular with a strained, halting clarity. She had been on her bicycle, using it the way she always had to get from one place to another, when an explosion tore through the area without warning. What she remembered most were not events in a smooth sequence but a few isolated moments that came back to her like photographs: the bicycle beneath her, the force in the air, and then separate, sharp images of body parts that had seemed impossibly close and unreal. She said that when she tries to tell what happened, she knows it happened, but the words will not come; the memory stays broken into pieces, with whole stretches missing, as if her mind can only hold fragments. Even now she can summon the scene only in snapshots, each one fixed and vivid, but not connected enough to feel like a complete story.

In the months that followed, Asha noticed that some things could pull her back into that day with startling speed. A sudden bang in the environment—a dropped object, a slammed door, any sound that resembled an explosion—could make her body go rigid before she had time to think. At times she would catch sight of certain body parts in a way she could not predict, and the image would strike her with the force of the original scene, leaving her momentarily shaken and unable to settle. Even a bicycle could do it: seeing one chained outside a building, hearing the bell, or passing someone riding one would bring her attention back to the violence she had once experienced while using the same means of transport. She became careful about where she went and what she noticed, not because she wanted to think about the event, but because the world seemed capable of opening it up at any moment.

By the time she had rebuilt her life enough to attend school and later work as an auditor, Asha had grown used to moving through her days with an effortful distance from herself. She spoke of feeling dead inside, as if the part of her that once responded naturally to life had gone quiet. She had come to believe that she was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined her, even though on paper she still functioned well. Before the trauma, she had taken pride in being precise, dependable, and sharp-eyed; now she watched herself struggle with the ordinary demands of concentration and responsibility and interpreted those moments as proof that she had lost something fundamental. She described herself less as a person than as an object that keeps being carried from one obligation to the next. That was how it felt to sit in the office at her auditing job, reviewing figures at a desk for long stretches, while the familiar sounds of the building could keep her tense and watchful for the next sudden bang. The work was still there, but her sense of herself in it had changed. What once felt like a profession tied to her competence now felt like a place where she was simply enduring.

Asha’s single life, like her work routine, had become smaller around these experiences. She did not frame herself as actively choosing distance so much as finding that she had less and less to offer others. Friends and family noticed that she seemed muted, and she could not easily explain that the feeling was not sadness exactly, but a kind of internal deadness that made even conversation feel remote. She was embarrassed by how often she had to pause when trying to describe the past, as though the missing pieces in memory mirrored the missing words in speech. By the time she sought treatment, it was not because the event had become more recent, but because the present kept colliding with it in these small, specific ways, and she was weary of being startled by bangs, unsettled by bicycles, and caught by the sight of body parts in places where she did not expect them. What brought her to therapy was the fear that this reduced, numb version of herself might be the only one left. More than anything, she wanted to find out whether she could still become someone who felt fully human again.
